title: Operation RAGEPILL: India’s First-Ever Captagon Bust Exposes a Syrian Trafficking Pipeline Running Through Indian Ports
excerpt: The Narcotics Control Bureau seized 228 kg of the ‘jihadi drug’ worth ₹182 crore at Mundra Port and Delhi — and arrested a Syrian national linked to Gulf-bound smuggling routes
body:
India has never seized Captagon before. That changed last week, when the Narcotics Control Bureau dismantled an international syndicate that was using Indian ports to funnel the synthetic stimulant to the Middle East — a drug so closely associated with conflict zones that it has earned the moniker “the jihadi drug.”

Under an operation named RAGEPILL, NCB agents intercepted 227.7 kilograms of Captagon tablets and 196.2 kilograms of Captagon powder at two locations: a consignment at Gujarat’s Mundra Port concealed inside a chapati-cutting machine bound for Saudi Arabia, and a second cache at a residential address in Delhi’s Neb Sarai neighbourhood. The combined street value, the agency said, was ₹182 crore.

**The Syrian connection**

A Syrian national was arrested in connection with the seizure. Investigators say the man operated as a logistics coordinator for a trafficking network that exploited India’s position as a manufacturing and transhipment hub. The drugs were not produced in India — Captagon’s primary production centres remain in Syria and Lebanon — but the consignment was routed through Indian ports to exploit less-scrutinised trade lanes to the Gulf.

The concealment method was industrial-grade. Captagon tablets were vacuum-sealed and embedded within the mechanical components of a commercial chapati-making machine, a piece of equipment that would attract no suspicion in a shipment bound for a region with a large South Asian workforce. A separate consignment disguised in wool bales was also intercepted.

**What Captagon is — and why it matters**

Captagon is a brand name for fenethylline, an amphetamine-type stimulant first synthesised in the 1960s to treat narcolepsy and attention disorders. Banned across most of the world by the 1980s, its illicit production exploded during the Syrian civil war, where it became both a revenue stream for armed factions and a combat stimulant for fighters. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime estimates the global Captagon trade at $10 billion annually, overwhelmingly concentrated in the Arabian Peninsula.

India had until now been absent from the Captagon map. That it has appeared as a transit point reflects a broader pattern: as traditional trafficking corridors through Turkey and Jordan face tighter enforcement, syndicates are seeking alternative routes through South and Southeast Asia.

**The Gulf diaspora’s stake**

For the roughly nine million Indians living in the Gulf states, the revelation that India is being used as a Captagon pipeline carries uncomfortable implications. The Indian diaspora in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Kuwait is the backbone of those economies’ service and construction sectors. Any association — however indirect — between Indian trade routes and drug trafficking risks reputational damage at a moment when India is aggressively courting Gulf investment and deepening bilateral ties through free-trade agreements and logistics corridors.

Home Minister Amit Shah, who announced the seizure, framed it as evidence of the government’s “zero tolerance” policy on narcotics and linked it to a broader crackdown that has included recent seizures of cocaine at Goa’s Dabolim airport and cannabis shipments intercepted at sea.

**Structural questions remain**

The Mundra Port dimension is particularly sensitive. The same port was the entry point for the 2021 Adani-linked heroin seizure of nearly 3,000 kilograms, one of India’s largest drug hauls. That Mundra has again featured in a major narcotics interception suggests persistent vulnerabilities in India’s port-screening infrastructure, despite investments in container scanners and intelligence-sharing protocols with the US Drug Enforcement Administration.

The NCB has said further arrests are expected and that it is coordinating with Interpol and Gulf counterparts. The investigation will test whether India can credibly position itself as a security-conscious trade partner — a claim central to its pitch for the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor.

For now, the seizure stands as a landmark: India’s first encounter with a drug it had previously only read about in dispatches from Aleppo and Beirut. That it arrived hidden in a chapati machine, bound for the same Gulf cities where millions of Indians earn their livelihoods, is a detail almost too pointed to require metaphor.
